newsitem.title: UK: Size of Labour win key for stg on "morning after".
newsitem.headline: Size of Labour win key for stg on "morning after".

text.p: "Sterling sanguine about Labour victory", "UK markets unfazed by prospect of Labour government".... are they really?
Or is there scope for a sell-off on Friday by investors still plagued by the ghost of "old Labour" of the 1970s with its image of high-spending, soaring inflation and high-taxation?
"There is a scale of risks, and it all depends on the size of Labour's majority," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Meggyesi said investors generally felt comfortable about the prospect of a Labour victory in Britain's election on May 1.

Latest opinion polls show Tony Blair's opposition Labour party 22 points ahead of John Major's ruling Conservatives. If such polls are correct Labour will win with a massive 265-parliamentary majority.
The party has worked hard to shed its "old Labour" image, and no drastic changes in macro-economic policy are expected to emerge after the election.
A Labour majority of between 50 and 100 should be pretty neutral but an outcome giving the party either a small majority or a landslide win could unsettle investors, analysts said.

The worst scenario would be a hung parliament, with no outright majority for either Labour or the Conservatives, which would make it difficult to enact legislative changes and pursue a consistent economic policy.
The market's fear of a hung parliament was evident when sterling slid earlier this month after one opinion poll showed a sharp slide in Labour's lead.

But that poll was a one-off, and unlike 1992 when the Labour party's lead in the last few days of the election campaign was only three to five percent. the current lead is averaging around 15 percent.

The City, London's financial district, might be sanguine about Tony Blair taking office as Prime Minister but a Labour victory is unlikely to be greeted with the same degree of enthusiasm in trading rooms as a Conservative winner.
In 1992, a wave of buying swept British markets after the Conservatives' defied predictions and returned to power with an overall majority.

"Deep down, the City would still prefer a Conservative Party victory but even the die-hard Tories (conservatives) see it as a foregone conclusion that Labour will win," said a senior trader at a German bank.

The day after the 1992 election, the British stock market closed over five percent higher the day after the 1992 election, and the pound gained almost three pfennigs against the mark and 2-1/2 cents versus the dollar.
The market euphoria even prompted the Bank of England - in an unprecedented move - to issue gilts in the middle of the election night. The new paper sold like hot cakes.

"It's different now - in 1992 the result came as a shock because Labour was expected to win," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi. "Now a Labour victory is fully discounted, and I don't think the world will be different place on Friday morning."
Yet, some residual doubt about Labour remains among some overseas investors, said Shepperd.

"In the U.S. and Japan, the election here makes less headlines, so there might be a lack of information about Labour's transformation but the big international players are fully aware of how Labour has changed," he said.

The big day for sterling is likely to come in the week after the election, when the finance minister and the Bank of England governor hold the first monetary meeting of the new government. A meeting is scheduled for May 7 but it might be postponed because it would be very close to the election.
"The market is expecting a 25 basis points interest rate increase then, and if that doesn't materialise soon after the election, there is scope for selling the pound," said Meggyesi at Deutsche.

Of much more immediate market interest will be the U.S. employment data out on Friday, traders said. If a strong non-farm payroll number sparks a dollar rally, sterling/mark should be riding higher on its coattails - as it has done during its sharp rise this year.
